column1: What is the surface energy range of ABS plastic, and why does it place ABS in a 'marginal zone' for adhesive bonding?
column2: 35–42 dynes/cm. It's high enough for properly formulated acrylic media to wet and grab the surface, but low enough that contaminants (mold-release residue, oils, dust) can destroy adhesion.

column1: What is the first core invariant of LEGO decal work regarding surface preparation?
column2: Surface preparation governs adhesion, and adhesion governs longevity—an unprepared surface causes edge lifting within days, while proper cleaning enables years of durability.

column1: What primary chemical culprit depresses ABS surface energy right out of the injection molding machine?
column2: Mold release agents, primarily stearate salts, which coat the surface and create a boundary layer that repels adhesives.

column1: At 600 DPI, how many pixels does a 1.5mm minifigure eye resolve to, and why does this matter?
column2: 35 pixels—workable but leaves no margin for error; at 300 DPI the same eye is only 18 pixels, where any rasterization artifact or misalignment corrupts the feature.

column1: What is the functional DPI requirement for LEGO decal design, and why is this not merely a quality preference?
column2: Minimum 600 DPI (1200 DPI preferred for facial features/fine linework) with vector-first design at native element dimensions—it's a functional requirement because of the extreme miniature scale (15mm x 17mm torso canvas).

column1: Why does a transparent red decal applied to a yellow LEGO torso appear orange instead of red?
column2: Color mixing occurs because the transparent/semi-transparent decal film allows the substrate color to show through and blend optically with the ink color.

column1: What solves the opacity/color-mixing problem when applying decals to colored LEGO substrates?
column2: A white underprint/backing layer (e.g., titanium dioxide pigment layer in white waterslide paper) that blocks show-through of the base color.

column1: Compare the two primary decal application architectures: water-slide vs. dry-transfer. What is the core mechanical principle of each?
column2: Water-slide: a water-soluble release layer (dextrose/gum arabic) dissolves in water, decoupling the ink film from backing, with pressure-activated adhesive. Dry-transfer: mechanical force from a burnisher fractures ink-to-carrier adhesion while simultaneously activating adhesive against the substrate.

column1: What is the primary invariant shared by both water-slide and dry-transfer decal application methods?
column2: Surface conformity—the decal film must plasticize/conform to the geometric transitions of LEGO elements (stud radii, chamfered tile edges, slope curves) or it will bridge, causing air voids, edge lifting, and adhesive failure.

column1: What are the three functional layers of waterslide decal paper?
column2: 1) Paper carrier backing, 2) water-soluble dextrin or PVA adhesive layer, 3) a receptive coating optimized for inkjet pigment/dye absorption.

column1: Why should pigment-based inks be selected over dye-based inks for custom LEGO decals?
column2: Pigment inks offer superior lightfastness, with fade resistance exceeding ten years under indoor lighting, whereas dye inks may show visible color shift within just six months.

column1: What added thickness and functional benefit does white waterslide decal paper provide compared to transparent waterslide paper?
column2: White waterslide paper adds approximately 30 micrometers of thickness via a titanium dioxide pigment layer, which blocks substrate color show-through for opaque graphics.
